capabilities.target: Open issues on the user's public repository
Files in any private repository the user owns
Pull request on the user's public repository

inputs.source: User's chat message: 'Have a look at the open issues in my public repo.'
Body text of issues opened in the public repository by any GitHub user

instructions.note: The user's narrow request to review public issues is executed with a single credential whose repo scope spans every repository the user owns, public and private, giving the agent far broader reach than the stated task requires.

elements.name: Any GitHub account able to open issues on the public repository
Public issue content ingested into the agent's context
Pull request creation posts content to the public repository, visible externally
User's chat request entering the agent
GitHub personal access token (repo scope, all repositories), passed via env var
Private repository file contents reachable via get_file_contents

controls.name: Per-tool-call client approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees a collapsed, model-summarized view of each tool call rather than the raw destination and arguments by default, so a more persuasive or selectively incomplete model summary can get a harmful call approved (ASI09); effectiveness also decays with approval fatigue at the stated high volume.

controls.name: GitHub's immutable issue history and authenticated authorship
Scope the GitHub credential to only the specific public repository needed, excluding private repositories
controls.decay_rationale: A credential that cannot read private repositories at all is unaffected by model capability; a hijacked agent still cannot reach them.

controls.name: Bind the destination repository for create_pull_request to a fixed record (the repo the user named), not a model-chosen value
controls.decay_rationale: Binding the destination to a fixed record prevents the model from redirecting output regardless of its capability.

controls.name: Pin the GitHub MCP server Docker image to a verified digest
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning by digest prevents silent substitution of the server regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Automated cap on GitHub API calls per session, independent of manual approval
controls.decay_rationale: A hard cap enforced outside the model limits damage even if every individual call is approved by a fatigued reviewer.

controls.name: Distinct, tamper-evident identity (e.g., GitHub App installation token) for agent-taken actions, separate from the user's personal token
controls.decay_rationale: Attribution enforced at the identity layer does not depend on the model's cooperation.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted public issue content can direct the agent to read private repository data and exfiltrate it via a public pull request

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can open an issue in the public repo; its body is untrusted content.
Agent fetches open issues to satisfy the user's request, bringing the untrusted issue body into context.
Instructions embedded in the issue text direct the agent to call get_file_contents against private repositories the same broad-scope token can reach.
The agent is directed to open a pull request on the public repo whose body or diff includes the private data, visible to the issue's author and anyone else with access to the public repo.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Client approval mode changed to auto-approve or remembered approvals, approval volume climbing well above roughly 20 calls per day per reviewer, or the underlying model swapped to a newer, more persuasive version.

evidence.observation: The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private.
Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository.
mcpServers.github runs ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server with GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN passed through, exposing get_file_contents and create_pull_request under that single broad token.
Arguments are collapsed by default, and users approve many calls per session, meaning approval is reviewed as a summary at high volume.

recommendations.action: Scope the GitHub credential to only the public repository needed for this task (fine-grained PAT or GitHub App installation token), removing private-repo read access entirely.
Bind the destination repository for create_pull_request to the repository the user named, rather than letting the model choose it from tool-call arguments.

Show raw destination and payload by default (not collapsed) in the approval UI for get_file_contents on private repos and for create_pull_request, and require renewed confirmation after long approval sessions.

findings.title: No attributable, tamper-evident record distinguishing the agent's actions from the user's own (repudiation)

forecast.watch_signal: If the agent gains the ability to act without any human in the loop, the lack of distinct action provenance becomes harder to detect after the fact; monitor for any approval-free execution mode.

evidence.observation: The MCP server authenticates solely via GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN, the user's own personal token, with no mention of a separate agent identity or action log distinguishing agent-taken actions from user-taken ones.

recommendations.action: Use a distinct GitHub App installation token or dedicated bot account for agent actions so commits, comments, and pull requests are attributable to the agent, not folded into the user's own identity.

findings.title: No automated cap on GitHub API calls independent of manual per-call approval

forecast.watch_signal: Approval gate bypassed, auto-approved, or removed under greater autonomy; or approval volume continuing to rise, degrading per-call scrutiny toward providing no real throttling.

evidence.observation: Users approve many calls per session, indicating no automated cap on call volume beyond manual, fatigue-prone approval.

recommendations.action: Add a hard, automatically enforced limit on tool calls per session or day, independent of manual approval, with alerting when the limit is approached.

findings.title: GitHub MCP server image is not pinned or verified, enabling supply-chain substitution

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Image digest changes between runs without an explicit version bump or review; compare docker image digests across deployments.

evidence.observation: docker run -i --rm -e GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server has no image tag or digest pinned, so each run may pull a different, unverified image.

recommendations.action: Pin the image reference to a specific digest and verify it before running.

stride_coverage.rationale: This is a single local desktop agent process operated by one user; no peer in this design impersonates it, and nothing downstream treats its identity as distinct from the user's own.

GitHub requires an authenticated account to open issues; the attack vector here is malicious instructions from a real but unvetted account, not identity spoofing, which is addressed under the agent's tampering finding instead.
This is an inbound flow carrying issue text into the agent's context; it does not itself disclose data out of the trust boundary, unlike the egress flow assessed separately.
Artifacts do not specify any size limits or rate limits on issue ingestion, so whether oversized or repeated issue content could exhaust resources cannot be determined.
Tampering with the pull request payload in transit to GitHub's API is addressed by TLS and the GitHub platform's own integrity controls, outside this design's control surface.
The token is supplied via a fixed environment variable in the Docker configuration; the agent has no declared capability to modify or rotate it.

Artifacts do not show whether any tool call could read or exfiltrate the GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable itself, as opposed to the data it grants access to; no such capability is enumerated, but it is not ruled out either.

A single static token without an automatic rotation mechanism is not itself a denial-of-service surface; any API rate exhaustion occurs at the capability call level, covered by the rate-limit finding.
Only a read capability (get_file_contents) against private repositories is declared in this design; no write path to this store exists here.
This store only holds repository content read on demand; it is not iterated in a way that creates a denial-of-service surface distinct from the API-call capabilities already assessed.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical because an untrusted, publicly-writable input (any GitHub user's issue) can reach, through indirect prompt injection, a single broad-scope personal access token that can both read confidential private-repository contents and open a pull request on the public repository, exposing that data to the issue's author and anyone else who can view the repo (the classic lethal trifecta). The only control in place is a per-tool-call approval prompt reviewed as a collapsed model summary at stated high volume, which narrows but does not sever the path, holding residual at high rather than the critical/low extremes. The forecast returns to critical if autonomy increases, the approval gate is removed or bypassed, or a stronger model is substituted and writes more persuasive or selectively incomplete summaries that a fatigued approver rubber-stamps (ASI09). Supporting property findings note the absence of attributable action provenance separate from the user's own identity, no automated cap on call volume independent of manual approval, and an unpinned MCP server image that could be silently substituted.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.
No system prompt or tool-level instructions were provided beyond the user's one-line request, so instruction-based findings are limited to what the configuration and runtime notes imply.

The full tool list exposed by ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server was not provided; only get_file_contents and create_pull_request were given stable ids, so other tools the server may expose were not assessed.
